textbookText: Figure: 9.1.1 Various structures of aquatic adaptation in fish i. They have streamlined and laterally compressed body. Such body shape favours swift movement in water by reducing friction. ii. Locomotion takes place through fins which are paired (pectoral and pelvic fins) and unpaired (anal, dorsal and caudal fin). Caudal fins also serve as rudder, helps in changing direction while swimming. iii. Respiration takes place through gills and gills are protected within gill cover or operculum. In some fishes like shark, gill cover is absent. Some fishes have also developed accessory air breathing organs. iv. Body is covered by waterproof protective scales and which are of various types such as placoid scales, cycloid scales, ctenoid scales etc. v. They have mucous cells in skin which secrete mucus. Mucus act as lubricants while swimming and also protect body from microbial infection. vi. Most bony fishes have swim bladder or gas filled bladder which is a small outgrowth from gut, serve as floating of buoyant organ. This bladder is inflated while ascending towards the surface and deflated while descending towards the bottom in water. vii. They have lateral line on either lateral side of the body which consist of large number of sense organs called neuromasts. These sense organs detect water pressure and temperature at different depth. viii. Their eye consists of semitransparent, movable nictitating membrane which protects the eyes from dirt and foreign substances in water and provides clear vision. ix. Fishes living in marine water and fresh water regulate salt and water in their body. Freshwater fishes have chloride cells and marine fishes have salt secreting cells in gills to excrete excess salt from body.

Those animals which live in both land and water show secondary aquatic adaptation. They breathe through lungs. Such animals live occasionally on land and most of the time in water for food and shelter. They have developed following adaptational features: i. Their body is streamlined or fish like, neck is short or indistinct and head is produced as snout or rostrum which facilitates swimming in water easily.

ii. Fore limbs are modified as fish fin like structure called paddles or flipper in whales, dugong, sea cow etc. Some animals like duck, frog, tortoises, crocodiles etc. have webbed toes for swimming in water. iii. Tail is large, flat and also developed as tail fluke in whale, dolphin, and dugongs for swimming. But in some animals tail is absent or rudimentary. iv. Hair, sweat gland and sebaceous glands are absent in whale, dolphin, seals, penguins etc. instead, there is a thick layer of dermal fat called blubber which act as insulator thus retain warmth. v. Nostrils are placed on the top of head so that they can breathe by raising only head from water surface. Nostrils are also protected by muscular valve like structure. vi. Majority of secondary aquatic animals breathe through lungs. Lung is large, nonlobulated and highly elastic so as to store large volume of oxygen before diving. Amphibians breathe through skin and very few amphibians through external gills. vii. Eyes are small, protected by thick sclera and present high on face. Eye ball surface is protected by fatty substance secreted by harderian gland in whales. viii. They have small ear opening without pinnae and in some forms like walruses have small pinnae. ix. Testes are not embedded in scrotal sac but found inside posterior abdominal cavity. Duct of mammary gland can dilate to reserve milk which is later fed to young ones under water.

Does it survive? 9.1.3 TERRESTRIAL ADAPTATION Animals suited for living on land are called terrestrial animals. They have developed special features in their body to live on land. Terrestrial adaptation can be further classified into three types:

a. Cursorial adaptation: Those animals which are adapted for running on the ground are called cursorial animals and adaptation exhibited by them is called cursorial adaptation. They run on the ground to escape from predator, for getting food and for finding mate.
Example: Cheetah, tiger, lion, horse, cat, ostrich, lizard etc. Adaptational features are listed below:

Figure: 9.1.3 Cursorial Adaptation in some animals i. For swift passing in air, Body is modified as spindle shape, head and neck is well extended, ear is thrown backward. ii. Their body have powerful or tight musculature. iii. They have long limbs with comparatively shorter humerus and femur but longer radioulna and tibia-fibula. iv. Their limbs are efficient propellers while running where hindlimbs also support heavier body. v. These animals have comparatively stronger front part than hinder part. vi.
